e.etymology: From Old French Denis, from Latin Dionysius, 'follower of Dionysus', the Greek god of wine. Saint Denis, patron of France, made it common, and the Normans took it to England.

assoc.t: Dennis the Menace, comic strip troublemaker

e.etymology: From Hebrew Avram, 'exalted father', from av, 'father', and ram, 'high'. In Genesis it is the patriarch's name before God renames him Abraham.
namesakes: Abram (the biblical patriarch before he was renamed Abraham)

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Violet, from violeta, the flower, which goes back to Latin viola.
From gold with the -ie ending, a pet name for a fair-haired girl that was popular in America around 1900. It also served as an English form of the Yiddish Golda.

assoc.t: Goldie Hawn, Oscar-winning actress
common pet name for goldfish and golden retrievers

e.etymology: From Arabic zayd, from the root z-y-d, 'to increase'. Zayd ibn Harithah, the adopted son of the Prophet Muhammad, is the only companion named in the Quran.
An elaboration of Jane with the French-style ending -elle, in use since the 20th century. Jane goes back through French to the Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
From the surname meaning 'son of Will', Will being a short form of William. As a first name it peaked in the US during Woodrow Wilson's presidency.
namesakes: Wilson Pickett (soul singer, In the Midnight Hour)

assoc.t: Wilson, sporting goods maker (tennis, footballs)
Wilson the volleyball in the film Cast Away
Woodrow Wilson, 28th US president
Wilson, the neighbor on Home Improvement

e.etymology: A 20th-century blend of Mary and Lynn. Broadway star Marilyn Miller popularized it in the 1920s, and Marilyn Monroe's stage name was borrowed from hers.

assoc.t: Marilyn Monroe, 1950s film icon

e.etymology: A spelling of Adriana, the feminine of Adrian, from Latin Hadrianus, 'from Hadria', a town in northern Italy that also gave its name to the Adriatic Sea.
From Arabic ahmad, 'most praiseworthy', one of the names of the Prophet Muhammad. Ahmed is the usual English spelling in Egypt and South Asia.
From Hebrew Avdiel, 'servant of God', a name in 1 Chronicles. In Milton's Paradise Lost, Abdiel is the seraph who refuses to join Satan's revolt.
A pet form of Emma, Emily and other Em- names, with the -ie ending. Emma is Germanic, 'whole, universal'; Emily comes from the Roman family name Aemilius.

assoc.t: sounds like the Emmy, television's top award

e.etymology: A 20th-century English coinage, taken either as a feminine form of Kendrick or as a blend of Kenneth and Sandra. It peaked in the US in 1987.
namesakes: Kendra Wilkinson (reality TV star, The Girls Next Door)

assoc.t: Kendra Scott jewelry

e.etymology: A spelling of Gemma, the Italian name from Latin gemma, 'jewel'. The J spelling is also taken as a feminine form of Jem, an old pet form of James.
An older spelling of Lily, the flower name, also used as a pet form of Lillian, from Latin lilium, 'lily'. It was most popular in the US in the late 1800s.

assoc.t: Lillie, a lead of Pokemon Sun and Moon

e.etymology: A short form of Penelope, the faithful wife of Odysseus in Homer's Odyssey. It was given as an independent name in the US mainly in the mid-20th century.
namesakes: Penny Marshall (actress and director, Laverne & Shirley)
Penny (character on The Big Bang Theory)

assoc.t: penny, the one-cent coin
Penny, the neighbor on The Big Bang Theory
JCPenney department stores, known as Penney's

e.etymology: A respelling of Milo, the old Germanic form of Miles. Its root is uncertain; it has been linked to Slavic mil, 'gracious, dear', and to Latin miles, 'soldier'.
From the noble title, which comes through French from Latin dux, 'leader'. It is a long-standing American nickname, as for John Wayne and Duke Ellington, and sometimes short for Marmaduke.
namesakes: John Wayne (film star nicknamed the Duke)
Duke Kahanamoku (Hawaiian surfer and Olympic swimmer)

assoc.t: Duke University and its Blue Devils teams
duke, a rank of nobility
Duke Energy, large US electric utility
dukes, old slang for fists (put up your dukes)

e.note: Also one of the most popular dog names in the US.

e.etymology: A pet form of Thomas, from Aramaic te'oma, 'twin', the byname of one of the twelve apostles. Tommy has been registered as a full name since the 19th century.

assoc.t: Tommy Hilfiger, fashion brand often called Tommy
Tommy, The Who's 1969 rock opera
Tommy Pickles, the baby hero of Rugrats
tommy gun, the Thompson submachine gun

e.etymology: A Scottish feminine form of Kenneth, which merges two Gaelic names, Coinneach, 'handsome', and Cinaed, often read as 'born of fire'. In the US it is also short for McKenna.

e.meaning: he who holds firm the good
e.etymology: The Italian and Spanish form of Darius, from Old Persian Darayavaush, 'he who holds firm the good', the name of three Persian kings.
From the English surname, from Old English leah, 'meadow or clearing', for someone who lived by one. In the American South it was often given in honor of General Robert E. Lee.
namesakes: Lee Majors (actor, The Six Million Dollar Man)

assoc.t: Lee, denim jeans brand
Robert E. Lee, Confederate general
one of the most common Chinese and Korean surnames

e.etymology: A Welsh pet form of Margaret, from Meg with the diminutive ending -an. Margaret comes from Greek margarites, 'pearl'.

assoc.t: M3GAN, killer AI doll of the 2023 horror film
Megan Thee Stallion, rapper
Megan's Law, US sex offender registry statute

e.etymology: From an English surname for someone who lived by woodland clearings, Old English rod. The Rh- spelling arose in the 16th century by analogy with the unrelated Greek island of Rhodes.

assoc.t: Rhodes, Greek island and site of the ancient Colossus
Rhodes Scholarship at Oxford University
Cecil Rhodes, British imperialist behind Rhodesia
Rhodes, frozen bake-and-serve dinner rolls

e.etymology: Several unrelated names share this form: Japanese hana, 'flower'; Arabic hana, 'bliss'; the Czech and Slovak form of Hannah, Hebrew 'grace'; and Korean hana, 'one'.

assoc.t: Hana, Maui town at the end of the Road to Hana

e.etymology: The Hebrew form of Rebecca, the wife of Isaac in Genesis, from a Semitic root meaning 'to tie or join'. In the US it is used mostly in Jewish families.

e.meaning: a deep blue dye and color
e.etymology: From the deep blue dye and color. The word came through Spanish and Portuguese from Latin indicum and Greek indikon, 'Indian', because the dye was traded from India.

assoc.t: indigo, the blue-violet color of the rainbow

e.etymology: From the London district on the Thames, Old English Cealchyth, 'chalk landing place'. It became a girls' name in the late 20th century and peaked in the US in 1992.
namesakes: Chelsea Clinton (daughter of Bill and Hillary Clinton)
Chelsea Handler (comedian and talk show host)

assoc.t: Chelsea, neighborhoods in London and Manhattan
Chelsea FC, London Premier League soccer club
Chelsea boots, an ankle boot style
Chelsea, Barbie's little sister doll

e.meaning: from the land of the lochs
e.etymology: From Scottish Gaelic Lachlann, 'land of the lochs', a name for Scandinavia and so for a Norseman. Long a Scottish name, it became a favorite in Australia before reaching the US.
namesakes: Lachlan Murdoch (media executive, head of Fox Corporation)
e.note: The ch is the sound in Scottish loch; Americans say LOK-lun, and many misread it as LATCH-lun.

e.etymology: A respelling of Nova, from Latin nova, 'new'. In astronomy a nova is a star that suddenly flares in brightness.

assoc.t: nova, a star that suddenly flares in brightness

e.etymology: From an English surname for someone who lived near holly trees. It had a first run as an American boys' name around 1920 and is now used for both sexes.

assoc.t: Hollis, Queens, home neighborhood of Run-DMC

e.etymology: A modern American name on the pattern of Tyree and Kyrie. It is sometimes linked to Greek kyrios and kyria, 'lord' and 'lady', the root of the prayer Kyrie eleison.
